title: Land conversion for solar facilities and urban sprawl in southwest deserts causes different amounts of habitat loss for Ashmeadiella bees
abstract: Land conversion for human use poses one of the greatest threats to terrestrial ecosystems and causes habitat loss for a myriad of species. The development of large solar energy facilities and urban sprawl are converting wild lands in the Southwest deserts of the USA for human use and resulting in habitat loss for desert species. This is in part due to the Southwest deserts being identified as having high renewable energy potential while urban areas expand into areas supporting high biodiversity. Previous studies have quantified development within some of these biodiversity hotspots, but none have investigated direct species-specific habitat loss for different species of pollinators. Native bees are poorly studied, and therefore it is difficult to know how much habitat has been lost. We quantified the amount of land conversion occurring between 2010 and 2015 in Clark County, NV, Mojave County, AZ, and San Bernardino County, CA to assess direct loss of potential-habitat for species in the Southwest deserts. Using Satellite images, we quantified the direct habitat loss to solar facilities and estimated other land conversion due to urban sprawl using USDA land cover data. We created eco-niche models in MaxENT for ten Ashmeadiella bees, to estimate the amount of direct, potential-habitat loss caused by solar development and urban expansion. Our data suggest species are not equally affected by land conversion in the Southwest deserts and direct, potential-habitat loss to urban sprawl is much greater than the loss due to solar facilities. Furthermore, our data show each species incurs different amounts of habitat loss to both solar development and urban expansion as well as between counties. These results should assist in pollinator conservation program development by illustrating land conversion can vary between local governments and pollinator species.

## **Land Conversion for Solar Facilities and Urban Sprawl in Southwest Deserts Causes Different Amounts of Habitat Loss for** _**Ashmeadiella**_ **Bees**

## Shaun M. McCoshum[1,2  ] and Monica A. Geber[1]

**Abstract:** Land conversion for human use poses one of the greatest threats to terrestrial ecosystems and causes habitat loss for a myriad of species. The development of large solar energy facilities and urban sprawl are converting wild lands in the Southwest deserts of the USA for human use and resulting in habitat loss for desert species. This is in part due to the Southwest deserts being identified as having high renewable energy potential while urban areas expand into areas supporting high biodiversity. Previous studies have quantified development within some of these biodiversity hotspots, but none have investigated direct species-specific habitat loss for different species of pollinators. Native bees are poorly studied, and therefore it is difficult to know how much habitat has been lost. We quantified the amount of land conversion occurring between 2010 and 2015 in Clark County, NV, Mojave County, AZ, and San Bernardino County, CA to assess direct loss of potential-habitat for species in the Southwest deserts. Using Satellite images, we quantified the direct habitat loss to solar facilities and estimated other land conversion due to urban sprawl using USDA land cover data. We created eco-niche models in MaxENT for ten _Ashmeadiella_ bees, to estimate the amount of direct, potential-habitat loss caused by solar development and urban expansion. Our data suggest species are not equally affected by land conversion in the Southwest deserts and direct, potential-habitat loss to urban sprawl is much greater than the loss due to solar facilities. Furthermore, our data show each species incurs different amounts of habitat loss to both solar development and urban expansion as well as between counties. These results should assist in pollinator conservation program development by illustrating land conversion can vary between local governments and pollinator species.

**Keywords:** Sustainable energy, pollinators, pollinator conservation, land use, ecology, land conversion

**Article Impact Statement:** This study quantifies potential habitat loss due to renewable energy and urban sprawl and illustrates the different amounts of land conversion occurring with governmental subregions of these deserts.

Anthropogenic land conversion allows societies around the world to support the ever-growing human population while simultaneously posing one of the greatest threats to terrestrial ecosystems. Land conversion causes direct habitat loss for many species and interrupts habitat connectivity, while also having synergistic effects with fire regimes, heat, and biological invasions (Wilcox & Murphy 1985, Noss 1991, Vitousek 1994). Measuring land conversion within ecosystems and eco-regions is common (Brooks _et al.,_ 2002); however, these studies generally quantify loss of non-species specific ‘habitat’ within ecoregions including the Amazon Forest, Great Barrier Reef (De’ath _et al.,_ 2012) and the Mojave Desert (Brooks _et al.,_ 2002, Hunter _et al.,_ 2003, Parker _et al.,_ 2018). Few have investigated impacts to specific species’ habitats within these regions or for species with unknown conservation status. In this paper, we adhere to the definition of habitat as an area with resources and environmental conditions that permit occupancy, survival, and reproduction for a specific organism (Hall _et al.,_ 1997); therefore, land conversion including urban sprawl, top soil and vegetation removal, and agricultural production cause habitat loss.

The Southwest deserts of the United State include the Mojave and the Colorado Sonoran Deserts. The Mojave Desert spans parts of Southern California, Southern Nevada, eastern Arizona, and into Utah, with the southern area intersecting the Colorado Sonoran Desert. Land conversion has increased in the past decade in the Southwest deserts because these lands were identified as having high potential for renewable energy production (Ong _et al.,_ 2013, DRECP 2015, Hernández _et al .,_ 2015), especially solar energy which is considered to be environmentally friendly (Tsoutsos _et al.,_ 2005). Energy infrastructure has been promoted in the region via federal public policy initiatives promoting utility scale renewable energy (Leu _et al.,_ 2008, Barrows & Allen 2009, Lovich & Ennen 2011), and is expected to continue for decades to meet energy goals like California’s 50% renewable energy target by 2030 (California Energy Commission 2015). Energy production joins a long list of activities causing habitat degradation, habitat fragmentation, and habitat loss in the Southwest deserts. Some specific threats include land development and construction (Bureau of Land Management, n.d., Lovich & Ennen 2011, Vandergast _et al.,_ 2013), invasive plants and fire (Brooks & Matchett 2006), as well as military training and recreation (Berry & Aresco 2014, DRECP 2015).

Although these areas have high solar energy potential, they are also biodiversity hotspots with 2,500 known species of plants and animals that live in the region and more than 100 are considered in peril (Bureau of Land Management, n.d.) with many insect species having unknown conservation status (CDFG 2009). Currently, of the 100 species in peril, only 29 species and subspecies are listed as threatened or endangered under the U.S. Endangered Species Act, (Allison _et al.,_ 2014, Bunn _et al.,_ 2007, Hernández _et al.,_ 2015). Inventories within the region recorded 689 bee species (Minckley _et al.,_ 1999, Griswold _et al.,_ 2006, Saul-Gershenz _et al.,_ 2012), for most of which there is little to no information on conservation status, and it is therefore unclear how these bees will respond to land conversion and development (Kuvlesky Jr _et al.,_ 2007, Lovich & Ennen 2011, Northrup & Wittemyer 2013, Allison _et al.,_ 2014).

At this time, solar facilities differ from urban sprawl as most solar facilities are kept completely denuded of vegetation (US-BLM 2009) while keeping pervious surfaces (personal observation) that may be suitable for native bee nesting (Minkley _et al.,_ 1999). In contrast, urban sprawl generally incorporates plants, both native and exotic, which have been found to provide suitable forage for some _Ashmeadiell_ a bees (McIntyre & Hostetler 2001, Hostetler _et al.,_ 2001) while also creating many impervious surfaces including roads, rooves, and parking lots, increasing local air temperatures (Stabler _et al.,_ 2005, Middel _et al.,_ 2014). Urban sprawl has also been documented to decrease biodiversity (Valiela _et al.,_ 2007; Rebelo _et al.,_ 2011), augment water regimes (Sheldon _et al.,_ 2019), local temperatures and soil moisture (Jiang _et al.,_ 2015) which is important for bee nesting and emergence (Stephen 1965, Stephen 1965a, Wuellner 1999), as well as sex ratios of native bees (Fitch _et al.,_ 2019). Due to these differences, our study quantifies and compares the amount of land conversion for solar energy and urban sprawl occurring in three contiguous counties. Our research also compares how much potential habitat is lost for ten _Ashmeadiella_ species and clarifies how land conversion in these deserts can affect some species more than others.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

To investigate the amount of direct, potential-habitat loss occurring in the Mojave Desert and Northern Colorado Sonoran Desert for different _Ashmeadiella_ species, we created species distribution models for ten _Ashmeadiella_ bee species and quantified the amount of land conversion that occurred between 2010 and 2015. We selected the _Ashmeadiella_ genus because: we col-

lected many specimens in our field work; the genus has numerous collection records with many GPS data, and there are a variety of species living in the Mojave and Colorado Sonoran Deserts. Due to many species having poor collection history, we narrowed our study to the 10 species that occur in this region that had enough GIS data to support MaxEnt models (van Proosdij _et al_ . 2016). The Mojave Desert and Northern Colorado Sonoran Deserts are located in three states, and Mexico, so we focused on the three contiguous counties in Arizona, California, and Nevada (USA) because local and state government incentives differ in attracting energy development. We then analyzed the potential loss of habitat caused by solar energy production compared to habitat loss from urban sprawl.

## _**Ashmeadiellaa**_

_Ashmeadiella_ is a genus of small, robust, heriadiform bees in the family Megachilidae with 55 known species (Michener _et al_ . 1994) and is thought to be closely related to _Osmia_ (Michener 1939). This genus is endemic to North America, mostly found in dry environments with both generalists and specialists (Michener 1939, Wilson & Carril 2015). Nesting behaviors include tunnels in wood, hollowed stems, under rocks, and excavated terrestrial tunnels (Michener 1939, Yanega 1994, Wilson & Carril 2015).

## **Solar Facility Data**

Location data were acquired from U.S. Energy Information Administration map, Form EIA-860 Annual Electric Generator Report, and digitized by hand in ArcMap 10.2. Data were then clipped to select facilities within the desert study region. Using Google Earth satellite imagery from December 2009, we identified and removed solar facilities constructed prior to 2010, which allows us to include portions of solar facilities that were later added such as Facility CM48, in Clark County Nevada. The constructed solar facilities’ footprints were measured using Google Earth satellite imagery December 2015, to calculate directly affected areas. These areas did not include new roads or power lines but focused on perimeter fences around solar arrays. Roof top solar facilities, like that of Mandalay Bay Casino, Las Vegas Nevada USA, were not included in our analyses because installation of these facilities did not disturb the desert.

## **Landscape Analyses**

Cropscape data layers from 2010 and 2015 were utilized to calculate land use change between 2010 and 2015 in Clark County, Nevada, Mohave County, Arizona, and San Bernardino County, California. We calculated habitat loss to development by creating binomial rasters where we recategorized all pixels of Developed/Open Space, Developed/Low Intensity, Developed/Medium Intensity, and Developed/High Intensity to 1, and all other categories to 0 in both 2010 and 2015. The June 2009 data were then subtracted from the 2015 data producing the final landcover raster of the area developed between June 2009 and 2015.

## **Habitat Models**

To create the potential habitat _Ashmeadiella_ may be able to thrive, occurrence data were obtained from The Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF 2016) and our own data from collections taken between 2004 and 2016 (United States Department of Interior: National Parks Service collection permits: MOJA-2004-SCI-0016, MOJA-2005-SCI-0007, MOJA-2006-

SCI-0039, MOJA-2007-SCI-0022, MOJA-2008-SCI-0006, & MOJA-2016-SCI-0019). Occurrence points were compared to their expected range, and none were found to occur unreasonably far from their expected range. Data were rarefied at 10km to reduce spatial bias, using the SDMtoolbox (Brown 2014).  Environmental data (30 seconds resolution) were downloaded from WorldClim (www.worldclim.org) (Hijmans _et al_ . 2005). Using the occurrence data (GBIF.org, 2016) for each species a clip window was made 2 degrees further in each North, South, East, and West direction from the furthest point to isolate environmental data and reduce correlation bias from areas outside the species range. Clipped data were analyzed via a correlation matrix to identify and remove layers that were strongly correlated (r ≥ |0.7|) (Boria _et al_ . 2014) starting with annual rainfall because many ground nesting bees are sensitive to soil moisture content (Minckley _et al_ . 1999), then elevation (Sunday _et al_ . 2010), followed by precipitation if it was not correlated, until layers with correlation values of r ≥ |0.7| were removed.

After correlated environmental data were removed, both the occurrence and environmental data were used in Maximum Entropy algorithm (MaxEnt v. 3.3.3k) which uses covariates at occurrence points to calculate the conditional probability for an organism to exist at these locations (Elith _et al_ . 2011). We created models for each species using the spatially rarefied occurrence data and the environmental data layers specified above. The models were run in MaxEnt with the following settings: ten replications with averages reported, with 10,000 maximum number of background points; regularization multiplier at 1; minimum training value, and cross-validate were also turned on. We converted each output raster into a binary layer, counting model outcome values of 0.5 and higher as suitable which has been used in previous studies (Cameron _et al_ . 2011, McCoshum _et al_ . 2016, McArt _et al_ . 2017).

## **Analyses**

Solar facility rasters were added to the landcover rasters to allow comparisons between habitat loss to solar facilities vs. urban expansion (Projection: NAD 1983 Contiguous USA Albers). Each species habitat model was used to select pixels on the landcover rasters within the potential habitat to quantify direct, potential-habitat loss within each county. The amount of land conversion identified to occur within each species’ potential habitat is expressed as a percent of total potential habitat within each county (Table 1).

## **RESULTS**

## **Land Conversion**

Between 2010 and 2015, 19,201 hectares of desert were developed in San Bernardino County, CA, 2,985 of those hectares were for solar facilities. In Mohave County, AZ, 10,879 hectares of desert were developed, with 100 hectares for solar facilities. In Clark County, NV, 23,281 hectares of desert were developed, 2,232 of which were for solar facilities (Figure 1, Table 1).

Direct, potential-habitat loss due to the construction of solar facilities in all counties, for each species, was less than potential-habitat loss due to urban sprawl (Table 1). In Clark County, NV solar facility development accounted for 0 to 9.74% of the total potential-habitat loss with an average of 6.9% per species, with urban expansion accounting for the rest. AZ had the least potential-habitat loss to solar facility construction, ranging from 0 to 1.56% of the direct, potential-habitat loss for each species, with an average of 0.78% per species. San Bernardino County, CA had the most solar facility construction, which accounted for 0 to 21.47% of total potential-habitat loss with an average of 13.96% for each species (Figure 1, Table 1).

Looking at the potential habitat for each species we studied, _A. breviceps_ had the most total potential-habitat loss of 1.68% in Clark County, NV and of 0.63% in Mohave County, AZ. In San Bernardino County, CA, _A. californica_ incurred the most total potential-habitat loss of 0.88%, but our models predicted _A. californica_ had the smallest potential habitat in the region totaling 2,787 ha (Figure 1, Table 1). The species that had the second most total potential-habitat loss in San Bernardino County, CA was _A. aridula_ , with 0.52%.

Using the total potential habitat loss in the county as 100%, solar energy development caused the most potential-habitat loss of 9.74% of for _A. breviceps_ in Clark county NV, 1.55% for _A. xenomastix_ in Mohave County, AZ, and 21.47% for _A. femorata_ in San Bernardino County, CA. Urban expansion caused 100% of the potential-habitat loss for _A. californica,_ in all counties. The second most affected species for potential-habitat loss to urban expansion were _A. gillettei_ with 90.85% potential-habitat loss in Clark County, NV, _A. aridula_ with 100% potential-habitat loss in Mohave County, AZ, and _A. aridula_ with 96.38% potential habitat loss in San Bernardino County, CA.

## **DISCUSSION**

Our project is one of the first to quantify the direct, potential-habitat loss for specific species in the Southwest deserts due to land conversion and illustrates how land conversion in this region affects species potential habitat differently. Our data suggest land conversion for solar energy is considerably less than land conversion for urban sprawl in this region and affects certain species more than others. For every species we studied, potential-habitat loss due to land conversion for solar energy was less than potential-habitat loss due to land conversion for urban sprawl, illustrating that both land conversion types are a threat to desert species. In all three counties, direct, potential-habitat loss to solar facilities was always less than 22% of the total potential-habitat loss, which could possibly be reduced by incorporating solar facilities into urban expansion. Land conversion also differed between governmental regions with more hectares converted in San Bernardino County, CA and Clark County, NV compared to Mohave County, AZ which suggests land conversion within these deserts is not equally balanced between governmental subregions.

San Bernardino County, CA had the most direct, potential-habitat loss for _Ashmeadiella_ species to solar facilities, whereas Mohave County, AZ had the least with only 4 facilities constructed between 2010    2015 (Table 1). Both Clark County, NV and San Bernardino County, CA experienced sizeable urban sprawl which added to the direct, potential-habitat loss of these species as well as created more energy demand. Our data, however, do not measure potential indirect effects such as loss of habitat connectivity, or how organisms can be affected by living near these land conversions.

Although solar energy can be established on rooftops, within cities, or on degraded lands, current trends of converting natural lands to large solar facilities is occurring and will continue for the foreseeable future. Our research does not address the type of solar energy nor the manner in which the equipment is installed, as there are reviews which have already compiled that information (Turney & Fthenakis 2011, Hernandez _et al_ . 2014, Moore‐O'Leary _et al_ . 2017). Our study quantifies the amount of land converted from natural lands to developed within each spe-

cies’ potential habitat. Our  approach  can be utilized for many other species and can be used to support conservation efforts or even argue that solar facilities should be integrated into urban developments to reduce habitat loss. Further research is necessary to investigate how wildlife respond to these facilities as there are many unknown direct and indirect impacts on wildlife and wildlife behavior (Lovich & Ennen 2011, Turney & Fthenakis 2011, Dai _et al_ . 2015; Gibson _et al_ . 2017).

In counties like San Bernardino where more than 20% of total direct, potential-habitat loss for some _Ashmeadiella_ species was due to solar facility construction, it may be useful to incorporate pollinator conservation practices or mitigations into the permitting process, such as keeping areas under panels vegetated (Semeraro _et al_ . 2018). Furthermore, studies have suggested that the pollinator habitats on private lands may be insufficient to compensate for habitat loss to solar construction (Cameron _et al_ . 2012), which indicates enhancing public land management and on-site mitigation policies will need to be considered to offset impacts to wildlife.  Conversely, in counties like Mojave County, AZ, or for species like _A. aridula_ and _A. californica_ that were more likely to be affected by land conversion for urban sprawl, conservationists may have better success focusing on improving habitats via other causes of land conversion.

As the global human population continues to increase, it will be more important to understand the environmental impacts solar facilities have and way to mitigate the land conversion. This research serves as a potential case study for measuring the direct habitat loss for species existing in any area where solar facilities are planned and illustrates the importance of looking at species’ ranges within biodiversity hotspots.
